summary: The note surveys Canadian Indigenous folklore and supernatural traditions, using case studies said to have surfaced since September 1, 2023. It covers the Wihtikow, Mishipeshu, Maritime ghost ships, the Northern Lights, Sasquatch, Nahanni National Park's headless men legend, and skin-walker tales. It argues that these stories are living narratives that preserve values, history and identity, and that respecting them supports reconciliation.
one_line: Overview of Canadian Indigenous legends, from Wihtikow to Sasquatch, presented as living narratives preserving culture, values and identity.
key_facts: Indigenous folklore is described as a living narrative that upholds values, beliefs and identity, not just a chronicle of past events.
In late November 2023 in Snow Lake, Manitoba, Cree Elder Jeannette Bison retold how her grandmother encountered Wihtikow, an evil, cannibalistic spirit that appears in Canadian winters.
The Wihtikow story serves as an allegory about greed and humanity being lost under pressure, and about nature versus human instinct.
Mishipeshu is a horned serpent revered by the Anishinaabe peoples of the Great Lakes area; it is considered a protector and source of great power.
Historian Sofia Cardinal's accounts from September 2023 reported Mishipeshu sightings near Lake Superior.
Mi'kmaq and other Maritime tribes keep oral traditions of ghost ships; the Northumberland Strait's fiery ghost ship was reportedly sighted by Prince Edward Island fishermen in October 2023.
Some Yukon elders describe the Northern Lights (Aurora Borealis) as spirits of the dead playing soccer with walrus skulls, and increased auroras since late 2023 revived these narratives.

Many Sasquatch sightings have been reported in British Columbia forests, most notably during fall 2023; skeptics call them hoaxes, while many Indigenous communities see Sasquatch as an embodiment of wilderness.
Nahanni National Park in the Northwest Territories is tied to a legend of an evil spirit named Naha and a tribe of warriors who beheaded enemies and then decapitated themselves.
Alexie Hunter's documentary released September 2023 revived the Nahanni tale by combining oral history interviews with archaeological findings.

Skin-walker legends, including in Inuit mythologies, describe people who transform into animals; a December 2023 conference on Indigenous folklore said they symbolize adaptability, survival and the bond between humans and animals.
The note concludes that understanding and respecting Indigenous tales is integral to reconciliation efforts and to celebrating Canada's diverse cultural landscape.
